pairs.question: How can Meyy help me as a teacher?
pairs.answer: Meyy generates a complete lesson plan and assessment for any NCERT chapter across five subjects: Social Sciences (Grades VI–IX), Science (Grades VI–IX), Mathematics and English (Grades III–IX), and The World Around Us (Grades III–V). You enter your available periods — Meyy builds a fully sequenced, NCF-aligned lesson plan and a matched chapter assessment. It reduces your planning time while ensuring every plan is traceable to the curriculum framework.

pairs.question: Can you explain what is meant by an NCF-aligned lesson plan?
pairs.answer: An NCF-aligned lesson plan is one whose elements are traceable to the National Curriculum Framework 2023. In Meyy this rests on three things: activities are drawn from the NCF-compliant NCERT textbook — nothing is invented; they are structured using NCF's Pedagogy guidance for your subject and stage; and every assessment item is derived from the learning outcome implied by a competency-aligned textbook activity. Meyy also holds the chapter's competency mapping with its justification from the textbook — evidence of how the chapter's content embodies the NCF competency framework. You will find it in the allocation report you can download when planning the year's periods, rather than on the lesson plan itself. How activities are sequenced differs by subject, because textbook architecture differs — the alignment does not.

pairs.question: How can Meyy help me as a curriculum planner or administrator?
pairs.answer: Meyy's Year plan — part of My Lessons — gives you a whole-year view of teaching time across all chapters for a subject and class. It shows how the annual period budget should be distributed based on each chapter's demand, surfaces chapters that are heavier or lighter, and tracks your actual allocation against the suggestion as plans are prepared. This gives a curriculum planner a defensible, curriculum-grounded annual plan — not a guess.

pairs.question: How can Meyy help if I am home-schooling my child or supporting self-study?
pairs.answer: Meyy generates a structured path through any NCERT chapter — activities sequenced to build understanding progressively, with clear learning outcomes at each step. The paired assessment lets you check understanding at the end of each chapter. A home educator or self-directed student gets the same NCF-aligned plan a classroom teacher would use, scaled to their own pace and available time.

pairs.question: How does Meyy ensure policy compliance with NCF 2023?
pairs.answer: Every Meyy output is traceable to NCF 2023. Competency codes from the NCF framework are embedded in the chapter mapping. Activities are drawn from the NCF Pedagogy document for the relevant subject and stage. Lesson plans and assessments are generated within a set of subject-specific rules — versioned, internally maintained documents that translate NCF policy into precise generation constraints. No output is generated outside these rules.

pairs.question: What is the common approach across all subjects to lesson planning?
pairs.answer: Across all five subjects, the mechanism is the same: the chapter's own content drives the lesson plan, the lesson plan generates implied learning outcomes for each activity, and only those outcomes pass through to the assessment. The organising principle — how activities are sequenced within a chapter — differs by subject, because NCERT textbook architecture differs by subject. The pipeline is universal; the logic inside it is subject-specific.

pairs.question: What is the difference between a competency and a learning outcome in Meyy?
pairs.answer: A competency is a durable cognitive ability defined in the NCF framework — for example, 'interpret historical sources.' It develops across many chapters over a stage. A learning outcome is chapter-specific and activity-specific: it names exactly what a student can do after completing one activity in this chapter. Meyy calls these implied learning outcomes because they are derived from the activity, not imported from an external list.

pairs.question: What is an implied Learning Outcome? How is it used across subject streams?
pairs.answer: An implied Learning Outcome (implied LO) is a precise, observable statement of what a student can do after completing a specific lesson plan activity. It is called implied because Meyy derives it from the activity itself — not from a published LO list. In all five subjects, implied LOs are the primary bridge between the lesson plan and the assessment: the assessment reads them to determine what each question must test.

pairs.question: Are lesson plans based on external learning outcomes? If not, why?
pairs.answer: No. Board-published or externally prescribed learning outcomes are not used as inputs. Learning outcomes in Meyy are derived from what each chapter's activities actually demand of a student — they are implied by the activity, not imported from outside. Using external LOs would disconnect the assessment from what was actually taught. Meyy's approach ensures the LO is a precise record of what happened in the lesson, not a generic curriculum statement.

pairs.question: Why does the NCERT textbook architecture differ by subject, and what is the implication for Meyy's design?
pairs.answer: Social Sciences chapters sprawl across multiple competencies in named sections. Science chapters are built around a central cognitive operation — occasionally two, where the chapter genuinely integrates distinct operations. English is structured around six language skill spines applied to each text. Mathematics has an innate progression of worked examples, activities, and exercises. The World Around Us is built around a child's observable world rather than around disciplinary concepts at all. Because the textbook architectures are genuinely different, forcing one planning template across all subjects would flatten those differences. Meyy uses five subject-specific sets of generation rules so each plan respects the textbook's own logic.

pairs.question: How are lesson plans generated in Meyy? Who writes them, and what is the role of AI?
pairs.answer: AI models generate lesson plans within a constitutional framework defined by humans, and those frameworks themselves reflect the policy guidelines in place. Every generated plan is verified for constitutional compliance by a human gate and certified accordingly before it is served to you. Deterministic methods are then used to serve it, which keeps the wait short and the cost of AI model tokens down.

pairs.question: How does Social Sciences plan lessons?
pairs.answer: Social Sciences chapters develop several competencies across named sections. Meyy walks the chapter section by section, anchoring each activity to a specific section of the textbook. Higher-weighted competencies receive more activities and more time. Each activity ends with one implied learning outcome — a single sentence describing what a student who completed that activity can now do. These implied LOs are the only input the assessment receives.

pairs.question: For Social Sciences, what are the three types of competencies and how do the lesson plan and assessment reflect the difference?
pairs.answer: Central competencies organise the chapter — their removal would dissolve its teaching logic. Substantive competencies are developed substantially across its sections. Present competencies appear once, in passing. In the lesson plan, the more central competencies receive more activities and time. In the assessment the same order holds: the more central the competency, the more fully it is tested. What exactly is asked differs between the Middle and Secondary stages.

pairs.question: How does The World Around Us (TWAU) plan lessons?
pairs.answer: TWAU chapters are organised around named textbook sections. Meyy walks these sections in reading order, anchoring one activity per period to each section's own content, tasks, and observations. Every period carries a dominant pedagogical mode drawn from the NCF's five prescribed approaches for the Preparatory Stage: Observe and Record, Hands-on Investigation, Discussion and Connection, Create and Express, or Reflect and Act. The chapter's two strands — a natural phenomenon and the human-cultural response to it — are developed together through this section sequence. Each period ends with one implied learning outcome stating the transferable skill the student has developed.

pairs.question: How does Science plan lessons at the Middle Stage (Grades VI–VIII)?
pairs.answer: Middle Stage Science chapters build one central cognitive operation through clear, ordered stages — from first encounter with a phenomenon to the highest-order thinking the chapter is designed to produce. Meyy derives this cognitive progression from the chapter and plans activities along its stages. Each stage ends with one implied learning outcome. Activities are drawn exclusively from the chapter's own experiments, exercises, and exploratory prompts — nothing is invented.

pairs.question: How does Science plan lessons at the Secondary Stage (Grade IX)?
pairs.answer: Secondary Stage Science chapters are planned section by section, following the chapter's own section order — not a designed cognitive arc. Every activity is anchored to a named section of the chapter summary; content from outside that section is not introduced. Each section produces one implied learning outcome stating the transferable skill the student develops. Where the chapter integrates two distinct cognitive operations across sections, both are reflected in the lesson plan. Activities are drawn exclusively from the chapter's content — nothing is invented.

pairs.question: Why does Science use fewer Core Competencies per chapter than Social Sciences?
pairs.answer: Science chapters are built as self-contained competency units — each is designed to produce one primary cognitive ability. In rare cases where a chapter genuinely develops a second, cognitively independent operation across its own named sections, a co-central competency is recognised alongside the primary one. Social Sciences chapters, by contrast, routinely sprawl across multiple competencies simultaneously, with different sections developing different thinking skills. Because the textbook architectures are genuinely different, the generation rules differ by subject.

pairs.question: How does English plan lessons? What are the six spines?
pairs.answer: English lesson planning is built on six skill spines: Reading for Comprehension, Listening, Speaking, Writing, Vocabulary and Grammar, and Beyond-the-Text. A chapter — a poem, a prose piece, a dialogue — is walked through all six spines, producing one implied learning outcome per spine. NCF competency codes sit underneath, but the teacher engages with spines, not codes. Each outcome is assessed more than once, and at more than one level of thinking.

pairs.question: In English, how does the spine structure align with NCF?
pairs.answer: The six spines directly correspond to the language competency domains NCF 2023 defines for the language subject group. The teacher sees the spine structure — which is how language pedagogy is naturally organised — while the platform maintains full NCF alignment underneath. This keeps the plan usable for teachers without requiring them to navigate the framework directly.

pairs.question: How does Mathematics plan lessons?
pairs.answer: Mathematics chapters have an innate progression: worked examples introduce a method, activities make it tangible, exercises drill it. Each chapter also builds on the chapter before it. Meyy respects this: each period is anchored to specific worked examples, activities, and exercise questions from the textbook, in order. Prior chapter knowledge is treated as the entry condition — the plan begins where the previous chapter left off, not at an abstract competency statement.

pairs.question: For Mathematics, why does Meyy follow textbook flow more closely than other subjects?
pairs.answer: Mathematics is the only subject where the NCERT textbook itself already encodes a rigorous progression. The worked-example sequence, in-chapter activities, and exercise sets are not supplementary — they are the method. Meyy co-opts the textbook's own architecture rather than overlaying an external structure. Departing from the textbook flow would introduce gaps in the method chain and undermine the coherence the textbook was designed to provide.

pairs.question: What is the role of stage-wise pedagogy in lesson plan development?
pairs.answer: The NCF Pedagogy document for each subject and stage specifies what kinds of activities are appropriate — inquiry-based approaches for Science, source analysis for Social Sciences, language task structures for English, and so on. Meyy uses the pedagogy document to govern how an activity is structured. The chapter summary governs what the activity contains. The two work together: pedagogy determines the approach; chapter content determines the material.

pairs.question: By following the lesson plans, how do I achieve stage-wise Curricular Goals?
pairs.answer: Each chapter is mapped to NCF competencies, and each competency is linked to a Curricular Goal. A Curricular Goal is developed across many chapters over a stage — no single chapter achieves it. By using Meyy plans consistently across the year, a teacher builds toward each Curricular Goal progressively.

pairs.question: Where do activities come from? Does Meyy invent them?
pairs.answer: Activities are not invented. Every activity in a lesson plan is anchored to a named section of the chapter — it must be derivable from actual textbook content. The pedagogical approach — discussion, inquiry, map work, experiment, group task — is drawn from the NCF Pedagogy document for the relevant subject and stage. The chapter content and pedagogy document together produce the activity. Nothing generic or unanchored is introduced.

pairs.question: Why is there suggested homework in the lesson plan?
pairs.answer: Homework in Meyy is not supplementary content — it is a deliberate extension of the period's cognitive work. Each homework suggestion is derived from the same chapter section and progression stage as the period's activity. It gives students time to consolidate or extend what the period introduced, without requiring additional classroom time. It is a suggestion, not a prescription — teachers adapt it to their school's homework norms.

pairs.question: Why is TWAU treated as a separate subject from Science and Social Sciences?
pairs.answer: At the Preparatory Stage, NCF 2023 does not separate natural and social world learning into distinct subjects. TWAU integrates both into a single inquiry-oriented subject. The textbook architecture is also different — chapters are built around a child's observable world rather than disciplinary concepts. Meyy therefore uses TWAU-specific generation rules rather than applying Science or Social Sciences logic, which would misrepresent how these chapters are designed to be taught.

pairs.question: What competencies does TWAU develop, and how are they different from middle-stage subjects?
pairs.answer: TWAU develops observation, description, classification, and simple causal reasoning — foundational cognitive operations appropriate for Grades III–V. These are precursors to the subject-specific competencies that Science and Social Sciences develop at the Middle Stage. Unlike middle-stage subjects, TWAU competencies are not differentiated by discipline — a single chapter may develop observation of a natural phenomenon and awareness of a community practice within the same activity sequence.

pairs.question: Why does the lesson plan not include time for assessment?
pairs.answer: The lesson plan uses the full period budget for teaching. Assessment is a separate activity designed to follow the teaching sequence — it is generated alongside the lesson plan but is not embedded in it. This is a deliberate design principle: teaching time is fully protected, and assessment is not allowed to erode it. The teacher chooses when to administer the assessment after the chapter's teaching is complete.

pairs.question: What is a Learning Unit?
pairs.answer: A Learning Unit is one period's worth of teaching — the building block of every Meyy lesson plan. The plan appears as a sequence of Learning Units on a progress rail showing what is done, what is current, and what lies ahead. Each unit carries its own overview, materials, teaching activities and homework, and — where applicable — assessment items. As you teach, you move the pointer forward, so Meyy always knows where each section stopped.

pairs.question: Why does my lesson plan not show learning outcomes?
pairs.answer: This is deliberate. Implied learning outcomes are derived from each activity and are reserved for the assessment — they define exactly what each question must test. The lesson plan shows what you and your students actually do: activities, materials, and homework. Displaying outcomes inside the plan would add framework language without helping you run the period. You will meet each outcome in the assessment, attached to the question that tests it.

pairs.question: What is the Year plan in My Lessons?
pairs.answer: The Year plan shows how your annual period budget for a subject and class spreads across its chapters. Meyy suggests a distribution based on each chapter's weight or effort index, and as you prepare lessons it tracks your actual allocation against that suggestion on an ongoing basis. Use it to see whether the year is running ahead or behind, and to decide how many periods the remaining chapters can receive. If the annual total itself looks wrong, the pencil on the Total periods row opens it for editing without leaving the screen.

pairs.question: What do we mean by Assessment in Meyy? What is the purpose?
pairs.answer: Assessment in Meyy is a chapter-scoped, formative tool — generated alongside the lesson plan and designed to test whether students engaged with the chapter's activities in the spirit of developing its competencies. It is not an exam. Every question is traceable to an implied learning outcome from the lesson plan. Its purpose is to help the teacher see where understanding has formed and where it has not, at the chapter level.

pairs.question: How is Meyy assessment different from exams administered periodically to students?
pairs.answer: Periodic exams are summative — they test retention across many chapters at a fixed point. Meyy assessments are formative and chapter-scoped — administered after teaching a single chapter or single unit, designed to reveal the quality of student engagement with that chapter's specific activities. They do not carry marks or contribute to certification. The teacher guide that accompanies each question is designed for diagnostic use, not grading.

pairs.question: Are Meyy assessments 'for', 'of', or 'as' learning?
pairs.answer: Meyy assessments are primarily assessment for learning — they give the teacher diagnostic information to inform what comes next. They are not assessment of learning (certification or ranking) and not assessment as learning (student self-evaluation). Every question includes a teacher guide that names the learning outcome being tested and — for MCQs — explains what each wrong answer reveals about the student's specific misunderstanding.

pairs.question: Why does the assessment test Learning Outcomes and not the competency directly?
pairs.answer: A competency develops across many chapters and cannot be fully assessed at the chapter level. An implied learning outcome is chapter-specific and activity-specific — it names exactly what a student should be able to do after one lesson plan activity. Testing the implied LO tests whether the specific teaching in this chapter produced its intended cognitive result. This keeps assessment honest and prevents generic competency questions that float free of what was actually taught.

pairs.question: Does the assessment cover the whole chapter?
pairs.answer: Yes. Since the Learning Units of the lesson plan are organised to cover the entire chapter, the assessment — which is derived from the lesson plan's implied LOs — itself covers the entire chapter. Assessment length is not capped: chapters with more competencies produce longer assessments.

pairs.question: Why does the number of questions differ across chapters?
pairs.answer: Assessment length is not capped — it reflects how much the chapter itself demands. A chapter that develops more, and asks more of students, produces more questions; a slighter chapter produces fewer. Length follows the chapter's content and never a target number, which is why two chapters in the same book can carry noticeably different assessments.

pairs.question: Where do I find the assessment?
pairs.answer: Inside the lesson plan itself. Each question is anchored to the Learning Unit whose teaching it tests — open a unit's Assess tab to see its items alongside what was taught. Units that anchor no question have no Assess tab. For a single consolidated document, generate the assessment as a PDF or Word file from My Lessons — together with the lesson plan or separately, and with or without suggested answers.

pairs.question: What do the four tabs on an assessment item show?
pairs.answer: Each assessment item has four tabs. Overview states the learning outcome being tested, with the question type, cognitive demand, and competency where recorded. Question is the class-facing view — stem, stimulus, and plain options — safe to project or read out. Answer holds the correct option or model answer with the diagnostic guidance, and appears only when populated. Inclusivity carries the scaffolding and extension suggestions. Students should see only the Question tab.

pairs.question: Why are assessments linked to units and not summarised at the end of the chapter?
pairs.answer: Because every question tests the implied learning outcome of a specific activity, Meyy shows it beside the Learning Unit that produced that outcome. You always see what a question tests and where it was taught — making review and re-teaching precise. Administration remains your choice: conduct a unit's questions when the unit ends, or complete the chapter and administer them together as one assessment.

pairs.question: Why are there sometimes multiple assessment items under a unit and no assessments for some units?
pairs.answer: Question count follows the chapter's own structure, not an even spread. A unit that produces several implied learning outcomes — or one whose outcome demands both a diagnostic MCQ and a deeper task — anchors several items. A unit whose work is consolidated elsewhere may anchor none; its learning is tested through a question on a related unit. Coverage stays complete at chapter level: every mapped competency is assessed.

pairs.question: How is the assessment rubric developed in Social Sciences?
pairs.answer: In Social Sciences, how central a competency is to the chapter decides how fully it is assessed. The competencies a chapter is built around are tested most thoroughly, including its extended and open-ended work, while those it touches in passing are checked more briefly. What is asked also differs between the Middle and Secondary stages, and where a section rests on a source, a data table or a graph, the question works from that source. Each question is shown beneath the Learning Unit whose teaching it tests.

pairs.question: How is the assessment rubric developed in Middle Stage Science (Grades VI–VIII)?
pairs.answer: In Middle Stage Science, the assessment follows the chapter's own cognitive progression. Early stages are checked for grasp of the ideas being introduced, later stages ask students to reason with them, and the chapter's most demanding thinking is where its most open-ended work sits. Every question traces back to what its stage was designed to teach. Multiple-choice questions carry diagnostic distractors throughout, with a teacher guide explaining what each wrong answer reveals.

pairs.question: How is the assessment rubric developed in Secondary Stage Science (Grade IX)?
pairs.answer: In Secondary Stage Science, the form of each question follows the cognitive demand of the section it comes from, not the section's position in the chapter. Sections that establish knowledge are checked more briefly; sections asking students to apply a method are assessed on the method itself; and sections demanding analysis or judgement call for extended written responses. Every question traces back to the section it is anchored to.

pairs.question: How is the assessment rubric developed in English?
pairs.answer: In English, each implied learning outcome corresponds to one of the six spines applied to the chapter's text. Each outcome is assessed more than once and at more than one level, so a spine is never judged on a single narrow question. A Reading outcome is tested on the actual passage; a Writing outcome through a task tied to that same passage; a Speaking or Listening outcome through a structured task you can run in class. Every question is grounded in the chapter's own text — nothing is generic.

pairs.question: How is the assessment rubric developed in Mathematics?
pairs.answer: In Mathematics, the assessment asks whether the method travels — each question is freshly written to test it in a context the student has not seen. Where the chapter's material allows, Meyy also points to a matching exercise in the textbook's own set, so you can check transferable understanding and textbook fluency side by side.

pairs.question: Within the approach to Maths assessment, is there a difference between the Middle Stage and the Preparatory Stage?
pairs.answer: Yes. At the Preparatory Stage the unit of work is finer. At Grades III–V each discrete task — a worked example, an activity, an exercise set — introduces or drills a distinct micro-skill, so the assessment stays close to those individual steps rather than summarising a whole period. That way you can see which step in a method a child has actually grasped.

pairs.question: How is the assessment rubric developed in TWAU?
pairs.answer: In The World Around Us every competency a chapter maps sits at equal depth, so none is weighted above another. What varies is the kind of question, which follows the way the period is taught — an observation period is checked differently from a making-or-reflecting one, and where a period aims at a physical behaviour the task is performed and judged by watching rather than written. Where answers depend on local context, a teacher note confirms that regionally varied answers are acceptable.

pairs.question: How are question types chosen in the assessment?
pairs.answer: Question type is prescribed by Meyy's rules for each subject — never chosen freely by the AI, and never varied question by question. What decides it differs by subject, because what a chapter is built from differs: in some it follows the competency being tested, in others the demand of the section or the stage of the chapter's progression. The broad details can be seen in response to subject specific questions in the Ask_Meyy.

pairs.question: What are MCQ distractors and how can they help a teacher?
pairs.answer: In Meyy assessments, every wrong option in an MCQ is written with diagnostic intent — it represents a specific, known misconception or reasoning error students typically make. The teacher guide for each MCQ explains exactly what a student who chose each wrong option most likely misunderstood. This turns a multiple-choice question into a diagnostic instrument: the teacher does not just see how many got it wrong, but why.

pairs.question: Do assessments have answers, and how are they different for closed questions (like MCQs) and open-ended ones?
pairs.answer: Yes. Every question carries answer support for the teacher, never shown to students. For closed questions like MCQs, the correct option is marked and each wrong option explains the misunderstanding it reveals. For constructed responses, expected answer elements or look-for markers describe what a good answer contains. For open tasks, the guide describes what a strong response demonstrates. Assessment documents can be generated with or without these suggested answers.

pairs.question: What is inclusivity and its purpose in assessment?
pairs.answer: Most assessments include an inclusivity note — a practical suggestion on two fronts: how to scaffold the question for students who are struggling, and how to extend the cognitive demand for students who need a higher challenge. This is embedded in the guide alongside the question, not in a separate worksheet. It gives the teacher a differentiation cue at the point of use, without requiring separate preparation.

pairs.question: Why do we not have a marking scheme for the assessment? How can I work around it?
pairs.answer: Meyy does not generate traditional marking schemes with point allocations because the assessments are formative, not certification instruments. Instead, every question has a teacher guide: for MCQs, it names what each wrong answer indicates; for constructed responses, it lists expected elements or look-for markers; for open tasks, it sets out the expected elements and the look-fors that mark a strong response. If your school requires a numerical scheme, you can construct one from these guide elements.

pairs.question: What is an open task and when does it appear?
pairs.answer: An open task is a constructed-response question requiring the student to demonstrate a competency in an extended, integrated way — a poster, letter, diagram, explanation, or role play. It sits where a chapter's most demanding, most integrative work belongs, so not every subject uses one and not every assessment carries the same number.

pairs.question: Can one question test more than one Learning Outcome?
pairs.answer: No — each question has exactly one source learning outcome, and it sits beneath the single Learning Unit whose teaching produced that outcome. A question may still draw on content from more than one section of the chapter where that is legitimate, and when it does, the teacher guide names the sections it reaches into. So what is being tested stays singular and traceable, even when the material behind the question is broader.

pairs.question: Should I conduct assessments alongside chapter teaching, at the end of each chapter, or at the end of term?
pairs.answer: Meyy assessments are designed to follow the completion of a chapter's teaching sequence — not at term end. They are chapter-scoped: every question assumes the student has completed all the activities of the unit(s) to which the assessment is linked. So they can be conducted at the end of the unit or chapter. Administering at term end would mix chapter content and reduce diagnostic value.

pairs.question: What are the three aspects relating to time when it comes to teaching in a school?
pairs.answer: Three time decisions shape teaching. First, the annual teaching time for a subject in a class — the total periods available for the year. Second, the periods available to teach a particular chapter within that subject. Third, the duration of a period — and a school may run more than one duration type, for example a 40-minute regular period and a 60-minute double or laboratory period. Meyy works with all three.

pairs.question: Does Meyy allow me to set all these three as per my requirements?
pairs.answer: Yes. You set the annual period budget for each subject and class, the periods for any chapter, and one or more period durations — all remain adjustable. To guide you, Meyy's own algorithm proposes how a given annual teaching time should be spread across the various chapters, based on each chapter's weight or effort index. The proposal is a curriculum-grounded starting point; every number stays yours to change.

pairs.question: What is the importance of defining an annual period budget for a particular subject and a class?
pairs.answer: The annual budget anchors everything downstream. Once Meyy knows the total periods available for a subject and class, it can distribute them across chapters in proportion to each chapter's demand — so no chapter silently consumes time another chapter needs. It also lets you monitor the year as you teach: how much time is committed, how much remains, and whether the remaining chapters fit the remaining periods.

pairs.question: Does NCF suggest annual periods to be allocated to various subjects?
pairs.answer: Yes. NCF 2023 recommends annual teaching periods for each subject, defined stage-wise — Preparatory, Middle, and Secondary. They are advisory in nature, not prescriptive: each school should consider its local context — calendar, timetable, and priorities — and set its annual budget appropriately. Meyy also makes its own suggestion, drawn from the teaching practice it has observed in schools rather than from the published norm — which is why the two figures can differ for the same subject and class. Whichever you start from, the number remains yours: set it to what your school actually runs.

pairs.question: Where do I set the annual periods for a subject for a given class in Meyy?
pairs.answer: From the “+” in My Classes, or from the pencil beside the total on the Year plan. Meyy starts you with its own calibrated figure for that subject and class, so there is nothing to work out from scratch — you either accept it or type the number your school actually runs. There is a single figure to give, the annual period count, and Meyy tells you what it works out to in teaching weeks so you can sense-check it. The budget you set drives the Year plan's chapter-wise distribution.

pairs.question: Where do I set the teaching time for a chapter?
pairs.answer: At the point of preparing the lesson: when you generate a chapter's plan, you enter the periods you plan to allocate for it, and the plan is built exactly to that budget. For guidance, the Year plan lets you look at Meyy's suggested distribution of the annual available time across the various chapters — and then monitor your actual allocation against it on an ongoing basis as you prepare lessons.

pairs.question: How do we set the duration of periods? Can I set more than one type of duration?
pairs.answer: Period durations belong to your class set-up, and Meyy starts you on the standard length for that class. To change them, open the “+” in My Classes and choose Periods a week: the screen that follows lets you split that week across period lengths. More than one type is fully supported — for example a 40-minute standard period alongside a 60-minute double or laboratory period. When you prepare a lesson you tell Meyy how many periods of each duration the chapter has, and it plans to that mix.

pairs.question: I have periods of different duration within a week. How does Meyy reckon this in suggesting a lesson plan?
pairs.answer: Meyy plans each Learning Unit for a specific period duration — activities and their phases are sized in minutes to fit the period they belong to. When your week mixes durations, you enter how many periods of each type the chapter has; longer periods receive proportionately more work. The plan therefore reflects your real timetable rather than assuming every period is the same length.

pairs.question: Will I be able to complete an activity within the time indicated in the phases in minutes?
pairs.answer: The phase timings are made as realistic as possible — they are derived from what the activity actually demands, not spread evenly across the period. Real classrooms still vary, and that is expected. The Learning Unit model absorbs this: if an activity runs over, carry it forward and begin the next period where you stopped — the pointer keeps your place. Treat the minutes as a well-grounded guide, not a stopwatch.

pairs.question: Why do some chapters get more periods than others?
pairs.answer: Period allocation in Meyy reflects how much classroom effort a chapter genuinely requires — not how long it is in pages. The measure of effort differs by subject: Social Sciences uses competency weight; Science, English, Mathematics and The World Around Us use an effort index built from signals specific to each subject's architecture. The result is a defensible default allocation the teacher or administrator can audit and override for any chapter.

pairs.question: How does Meyy suggest periods for various chapters for Social Sciences?
pairs.answer: A Social Sciences chapter's demand comes from the competencies it develops and how central each one is to the chapter. The more competencies a chapter carries, and the more of them are central to its teaching logic, the larger its share of the year. A chapter built around several central competencies therefore receives substantially more periods than one that touches a single competency in passing.

pairs.question: How does Meyy suggest periods for various chapters for Science?
pairs.answer: Science chapters are weighted by how much classroom work the chapter itself demands — read from its own exercises, activities and demonstrations rather than from its page count. Chapters that ask more doing of students, and more demanding thinking, receive more periods. The same measure is applied to every chapter in the year, so the shares are comparable — and it is a starting point you can change for any chapter.

pairs.question: How does Meyy suggest periods for various chapters for English?
pairs.answer: English chapters are weighted by how much language work the text actually calls for. A chapter carrying a substantial writing task and an extended project demands more classroom time than one worked mainly through reading and discussion, and the allocation reflects that.

pairs.question: How does Meyy suggest periods for various chapters for Mathematics?
pairs.answer: Mathematics chapters are weighted by what the textbook itself signals — the density and difficulty of its worked examples, activities and exercises. A chapter that introduces several methods and drills them heavily draws more periods than one extending a method already learnt. The allocation reflects how much the textbook signals a chapter requires.

pairs.question: How does Meyy suggest periods for various chapters for TWAU?
pairs.answer: The World Around Us chapters are weighted by how much observing, making and doing they ask of a young child. A chapter built around field observation with a craft or project outcome draws more periods than one worked mainly through reading and talk. The allocation can be adjusted for any chapter.

pairs.question: What is competency weight in Social Sciences?
pairs.answer: Not every competency a chapter touches matters equally to it. Some are what the chapter is for — remove them and its teaching logic collapses. Others are developed substantially across its sections. Others appear once, in passing. Meyy distinguishes these three levels — Central, Substantive and Present — by examining how the chapter is actually built, rather than by judging which topic is more important. The lesson plan gives the higher levels more activities and more time, and the assessment tests them more fully.

pairs.question: What is the effort index?
pairs.answer: The effort index is Meyy's measure of how much classroom effort a chapter requires — used for Science, Mathematics, English and The World Around Us, the subjects where demand is best read from what a chapter asks students to do. It is worked out once from the chapter's own content, when the chapter is analysed, and Meyy's suggested period allocation is based on it. You never need to look at it: what you see is the suggestion in periods, and you can change that.

pairs.question: Why does assessment not have time allocated to it within the chapter period budget?
pairs.answer: The period budget you enter is used fully for teaching — the assessment is generated alongside the plan but never eats into it. If you intend to administer the formative assessment in class, reduce that time before inputting the periods available for teaching the chapter. Note also that NCF's recommended annual teaching time excludes time allocated for summative examinations, so your annual budget should represent teaching time alone.

pairs.question: What if I ask for too many periods — more than the chapter's fullest plan?
pairs.answer: Meyy serves the fullest plan it holds for that chapter and returns the surplus to your budget, naming the periods and minutes that came back. It does not pad a plan to fill time it was not designed for — those periods are yours to give to another chapter.

pairs.question: What if I ask for far fewer periods than the chapter needs?
pairs.answer: If you ask for fewer periods than a chapter needs, Meyy warns you. It fits the plan to the periods you have and additionally supplies the material for the sections that had to be dropped, so nothing is silently lost — that extra material is on screen only, not part of the exported document. If the number is far below what the chapter can carry coherently, Meyy instead names the minimum to plan for, rather than serving a plan it cannot stand behind.

pairs.question: Is there a maximum number of periods I can enter for one chapter?
pairs.answer: Yes — thirty for a single chapter. It is a guard against a slipped keystroke, not a teaching rule: no chapter needs anywhere near that many.

pairs.question: What are the two main tabs in Meyy and what does each do?
pairs.answer: Meyy has two main tabs. My Classes is home — a card for each section you teach, showing its current chapter and how far you have progressed; tap a card to continue teaching. My Lessons is the repository — every lesson plan you have prepared, with its assessment and the Year plan view. '+ Prepare Lesson' is available in both tabs whenever you want to plan a new chapter. Your subjects, classes and durations are listed behind the Settings gear, and the “+” in My Classes is where you change them.

pairs.question: How do I generate and download PDF or Word documents of my lesson plan and assessment?
pairs.answer: Click the My Lessons tab and choose the document image on bottom right of the lesson plan card. You can generate the lesson plan and the assessment together in one document or as separate documents, in PDF or Word format. For the assessment, you choose whether to include the suggested answers and teacher guidance, or produce a clean version without them for use with students. A fresh document can be generated at any time from the saved plan.

pairs.question: How does Meyy remember where I stopped my teaching with a particular section?
pairs.answer: Every section card carries its own lesson pointer. As you finish a Learning Unit, you move the pointer forward, and Meyy records it for that section independently — 6A and 6B can follow the same lesson plan and still stand at different units. When you return, each card shows exactly where that section is, and opening it takes you straight to the current unit. No dates or deadlines are involved — only where you stopped.

pairs.question: How do I add another class, section, or subject?
pairs.answer: The big “+” button in My Classes is the way. It opens a Subject · Class · Section chooser and walks you through the same short steps as your first lesson; the same “+” is also where you change your periods a week and your annual period budget. Settings › Teaching profile shows everything you teach and, behind its pencil, lets you add or remove a whole subject — but classes and sections are always added from the “+”. New section cards appear in My Classes as soon as a lesson is attached.

pairs.question: How do I set up my class profile in Meyy?
pairs.answer: Your class profile holds what you teach: subjects, classes, sections, period durations, and the annual period budget for each subject and class. You never fill it in upfront — it builds itself as you work, each lesson you prepare adding its subject, class and section. Settings › Teaching profile is where you read it whole. To change any of it, use the “+” in My Classes: class, section, periods a week and annual period budget each have their own row there, and each changes only itself. Meyy fills in sensible starting values — the standard period length for the class, and its calibrated annual budget — so nothing is ever left blank.

pairs.question: Can I rename my sections, or give them my own names?
pairs.answer: Yes. When you pick or edit your sections you can give any of them a short name of your own, up to eight characters — Rose, Lotus, whatever your school uses. Meyy goes on showing the class and section, 6A, with your name in fine print beneath it, so renaming disturbs nothing you have already attached to that section.

pairs.question: Where are my saved plans stored?
pairs.answer: Saved plans live in your Meyy account and appear in My Lessons, organised by subject and class. Each entry holds the lesson plan and, once generated, its assessment — linked under the same chapter record with a timestamp. Your plans are private to your account: sign in from any device and they are all there. No other teacher can see or change them.

pairs.question: Can I use Meyy on my phone or tablet?
pairs.answer: Yes — Meyy is designed mobile-first. Every screen is built to work comfortably on a phone held vertically, one-handed, during the school day: checking your classes, moving the lesson pointer, reading a Learning Unit before walking in. Tablets and desktops present the same experience with more room, which some teachers prefer for reading full plans or generating documents. Nothing requires a computer.

pairs.question: How do I archive lesson plans?
pairs.answer: From My Lessons: each lesson card carries an archive button. Archiving removes the plan from your active list without deleting it — the plan, its assessment and any notes stay stored, and the archive folder at the top of My Lessons holds them, each with a Restore button. Use it at year end to clear completed chapters while keeping the record. Archived plans stay private to your account, like everything else.

pairs.question: What happens at the end of the academic year?
pairs.answer: Meyy re-authorises its lesson plans for every subject and stage ahead of the new school year, and releases the updated edition at the end of the academic year — while every plan you already hold stays available to you. Moving to the new year is your choice, not something done to you: when you cut over, your class list carries forward untouched, your section bookmarks reset for a fresh start, and the previous year's plans and notes stay in your archive. Your subscription runs on its own dates, separate from this.

pairs.question: What are Chapter Notes? Where can I access them?
pairs.answer: Chapter Notes are your private jottings for your future self — one note per chapter, for the academic year. Open them from the ochre “Notes” bookmark in the margin of the chapter view. The note belongs to the chapter itself, not to any one section, so the same note is waiting for you whichever section you are teaching, and it is there when you preview the plan. It is saved to your account, so it follows you to any device, and it travels with your plans when you export them.

pairs.question: Is there a guided tour that explains the basic features of Meyy?
pairs.answer: Yes. When your first lesson is ready, Meyy offers a guided tour that points out the essentials on the live screen — your section cards, the lesson pointer, the Learning Unit tabs, preparing a new lesson, the documents you can generate, and the archive. It runs about twenty short steps, you can skip it at any point, and at the end Meyy asks whether the section it started you with is the right one. For anything the tour does not cover, Ask Meyy — this helpline — is available throughout the app.

pairs.question: Is Meyy free? What does the trial cover?
pairs.answer: Meyy offers a free trial that opens every subject and stage it covers. You may prepare any three chapters of your choosing, and re-prepare those same chapters as often as you like — trying a chapter at twelve periods and again at sixteen costs you nothing. There is no time limit: the trial is measured in chapters, never in days.

pairs.question: What exactly am I buying, and how much does it cost?
pairs.answer: One subscription lets you prepare unlimited lesson plans and assessments for one subject within one stage. Meyy serves three stages: Preparatory, Middle and Secondary. If you subscribe to Science–Middle, you may prepare unlimited Science plans for Classes 6, 7 and 8. To prepare Science for a secondary class — 9, and 10 when it is ready — you would take an additional Science–Secondary subscription. What a subscription costs is shown on the subscribe screen before you pay; the price is per subject-stage, for the year.

pairs.question: What happens if I do not renew my subscription?
pairs.answer: Your plans remain yours: you can open, export, print and archive every one of them. What stops is Meyy's working half — preparing new lessons, the progress tracker, and writing notes. Everything you already wrote stays, and can still be read and exported. Renew, and the working half returns as it was.

pairs.question: How do I add a subject I have not subscribed to?
pairs.answer: Your choosers show only the subjects and classes your subscription covers, so the profile stays uncluttered. When you try to add one outside it, Meyy says plainly that it is a separate subscription and offers it to you there and then. It never lets you add a subject first and asks for payment afterwards.

pairs.question: Where do I see my subscription and my invoices?
pairs.answer: Settings › Subscription & billing. Each subject-stage you have bought has its own card with its own expiry date, most recent first, and the invoice for the purchase that paid for it. Subscriptions that have ended stay listed — that card is the explanation for anything you can no longer prepare in.

pairs.question: How do I sign in? What is my Meyy account?
pairs.answer: Your mobile number is your Meyy account. You sign in by entering it and confirming the one-time password sent to you; there is no separate username or password to remember. Because the number is the identity, your plans, progress and notes follow it to whichever device you sign in on.

pairs.question: What am I agreeing to when I subscribe?
pairs.answer: Five acknowledgements, each confirmed separately, and then the agreement itself. In short: Meyy is a teaching aid and replaces neither the textbook nor you; it is not endorsed by NCERT, CBSE or any government authority; you must never enter students' personal information; its content is AI-assisted and may contain errors or change over time; and your licence is personal to you.

pairs.question: Where can I read the user agreement again?
pairs.answer: Settings › Legal, at any time — the full agreement and the privacy notice, in the same words you agreed to.

pairs.question: How do I get help, or contact Meyy support?
pairs.answer: For how something works, Ask Meyy — this guide — is the fastest answer. For anything else, open Settings › Support: choose what your message is about, write it, and send. A reference number appears on screen at once and reaches you by email with the reply window we work to. We reply by email, and it is the one channel we use, so nothing is lost in a chat window.

pairs.question: Can I download or export all my Meyy data?
pairs.answer: Yes — Settings › Your data & export gives you everything Meyy keeps for you in a single document, as Word or PDF: your account and teaching profile, your prepared plans and their progress, your chapter notes, your subscription record and your support messages. The Word version is ordinary and editable; nothing is locked.

pairs.question: How do I delete my account, and what is kept?
pairs.answer: Settings › Account › Delete my account. Meyy first offers you a download of your data, then asks you to type a confirmation — deletion is permanent and immediate. Everything of yours goes: profile, plans, progress, notes, support messages. Two things are deliberately kept, and neither holds any teaching content — the record that you accepted the user agreement, and the seller's invoice and reference numbering.

pairs.question: Can Meyy tell me which student has mastered which competency?
pairs.answer: No. Meyy generates lesson plans, assessments, and teacher guides — it does not process student responses or maintain individual student records. The assessment output tells you what each question tests and what each wrong answer reveals, but recording student performance, tracking mastery, or generating progress reports is outside Meyy's scope. Meyy is a planning and generation tool, not a student information system.

pairs.question: Can Meyy generate marking schemes?
pairs.answer: Meyy does not generate traditional marking schemes with point allocations. Instead, every question comes with a teacher guide: for MCQs, it names what each wrong answer indicates; for constructed responses, it lists expected answer elements or look-for markers; for open tasks, it sets out the expected elements and look-fors that mark a strong response. If your school requires a numerical scheme, you would construct it from the guide content.

pairs.question: Can Meyy track individual student performance?
pairs.answer: No. Meyy does not track, record, or profile individual students. It generates teaching and assessment tools for the teacher — it does not manage student data of any kind. Individual student tracking, progress records, and performance databases are outside Meyy's scope entirely.

pairs.question: Can Meyy prepare students for Board exams?
pairs.answer: No. Meyy generates chapter-scoped formative assessments aligned to NCF 2023 competencies. Board examination preparation — which involves summative testing, past paper practice, and exam-style question formats — is a different function. Meyy is not designed for it and does not produce Board exam preparation materials.

pairs.question: Can Meyy generate a summative test or term-end exam?
pairs.answer: No. Meyy generates formative assessments only — chapter-scoped, designed for a single session, and intended as a professional teaching tool rather than a certification instrument. Summative tests, term-end exams, half-yearly and annual examinations are outside Meyy's scope.

pairs.question: Can Meyy generate lesson plans for subjects not in NCERT — for example, a school's own curriculum?
pairs.answer: No. Meyy's pipeline is built entirely on NCERT textbook content and NCF 2023 competency mapping. It requires an NCERT chapter as its content input. Non-NCERT curricula — school-designed courses, alternative textbooks, or international curricula — are outside Meyy's scope.

pairs.question: Can Meyy generate a Holistic Progress Card input?
pairs.answer: No. Holistic Progress Cards are multi-dimensional, cross-subject instruments designed for whole-child reporting — they require inputs that go well beyond what a chapter-scoped assessment can provide. HPC generation is explicitly outside Meyy's scope.

pairs.question: Can Meyy suggest visual aids, worksheets, or physical materials for a lesson?
pairs.answer: Meyy supplies the material a chapter's activities call for. Each Learning Unit lists what its period needs, and a Material tab carries the prepared content itself — reference tables, card sets and prose references — which appear on screen and travel into the exported documents. What Meyy does not do is design worksheets or produce printable classroom graphics, and it does not decide how you resource your room. The plan gives you the substance; how you put it in front of the class stays yours.

pairs.question: Can Meyy tell me whether my school is NCF 2023 compliant?
pairs.answer: No. Meyy generates NCF-aligned lesson plans and assessments — it is not a compliance auditing tool. Whether a school is NCF 2023 compliant depends on many factors beyond lesson plan generation. Meyy management can discuss how the platform contributes to alignment, but compliance determination is outside the platform's scope.

pairs.question: Can Meyy generate multi-session projects or cross-subject tasks?
pairs.answer: No. Every assessment task Meyy generates must be completable in a single session with no external coordination. Multi-session projects, cross-subject integrated tasks, field visits, external speakers and anything needing community involvement are outside its assessment scope. The boundary is time and coordination rather than materials: a task may well call for physical materials and some teacher preparation, as Science regularly does. This keeps every assessment executable by any teacher, in any school, within a normal period.

pairs.question: Can Meyy generate content in regional languages?
pairs.answer: Meyy's generated lesson plans and assessments are currently in English. Ask Meyy — this help feature — answers from Meyy's curated knowledge base; it is available in English today, with additional Indian languages planned as the knowledge base is translated. Generation of lesson plans and assessments in regional-language mediums is not currently available.

pairs.question: Why does Meyy not cover the Foundational Stage?
pairs.answer: The Foundational Stage is built on play-based, experiential learning — the child learns through free exploration, storytelling, and guided play rather than structured classroom activities. Meyy generates lesson plans and assessments anchored to textbook sections and period schedules, which is a classroom-based pedagogical model. In our view, imposing this structure on the Foundational Stage would work against the spirit of how young children learn best. We have therefore chosen not to extend the platform to Foundational Stage.

pairs.question: Why does Meyy not cover some classes?
pairs.answer: Meyy plans to cover Classes 3 to 10. Its pipeline is built entirely on NCF 2023-compliant NCERT textbooks — every plan is anchored to their chapters and competency architecture — so it extends only to the classes for which that material exists. As and when the remaining NCF-compliant books are released, Meyy will endeavour to cover them within the earliest possible timeframe.

pairs.question: Does Meyy send reminders or notifications?
pairs.answer: No — by design. Meyy never asks 'what is due?'; it answers 'where did I stop?'. There are no deadlines, no overdue flags, and no notifications pushing you along. Your timetable is cyclic and your pace is your own: each section's pointer simply holds your place until you return. Teaching runs on the teacher's judgement, not on the tool's calendar.

pairs.question: Can Meyy hold my school timetable?
pairs.answer: No. Meyy deliberately keeps no timetable, calendar, or day grid. The only time facts it stores are numbers: period durations, periods per week, and the annual budget for each subject-class. That is enough to plan lessons and track progress without duplicating your school's timetable, which lives — and changes — at school. Where you are in a chapter is tracked by the pointer, not by dates.

pairs.question: Can anyone else see my plans and notes?
pairs.answer: No. Your plans, progress, and notes are private to your account — no other teacher and no administrator can view them. In turn, please be privacy-conscious in what you write: avoid using students' names or other identifying or confidential details in Chapter Notes or anywhere else on the platform. Refer to situations rather than individuals, so your records never carry information with privacy implications.

pairs.question: Can I edit the lesson plan itself?
pairs.answer: Not on screen — the plan you are served is fixed, so that what you teach from is the plan that was certified. You can export any lesson plan as a Word document from My Lessons and amend that copy however you wish. Chapter Notes are the one place inside Meyy where you write.

pairs.question: Can I get a refund if I do not like the plans?
pairs.answer: Refunds are considered for verified technical failure — a persistent inability to reach what you paid for. Dissatisfaction with the content or the pedagogy is not a refund ground, and that is exactly why the trial exists and why we suggest using it first: three chapters, unlimited attempts, no time limit, so you can judge Meyy properly before any money changes hands.
